newsitem.title: UK: British Moslems want Bill of Rights after election.
newsitem.headline: British Moslems want Bill of Rights after election.

text.p: Britain's two million Moslems called on the winner of Thursday's general election to outlaw religious discrimination and adopt a Bill of Rights.

Britain's ethnic minorities traditionally vote overwhelmingly for the opposition Labour Party but Moslem leaders hoping to win concessions from the new government were careful to steer a neutral course.
"As a religious organisation, we have not made a recommendation on which party to vote for," said Dr Syed Aziz Pasha, general secretary of the Union of Moslem Organisations.
"This is the only way we can be even-handed as we need bipartisan support," he told a news conference on Monday that opened with a recitation from the Koran.
Mohammed Sarwar is standing for the Labour Party in the newly formed Glasgow Govan constituency in Scotland. He is likely to be the first Moslem elected to the British parliament.

After an election that Labour are strongly expected to win, Pasha urged the new parliament to outlaw religious discrimination. "We suffer from racial and religious discrimination. We are victims of both," he told reporters.
Most of Britain's Moslems came from Pakistan and Bangladesh after World War Two. A second wave came in the 1960s from Cyprus, Morocco, Egypt, Turkey, Nigeria, Ghana, Iraq and Iran.
Pasha carefully avoided commenting on Iran's religious edict or fatwa calling for the death of British author Salman Rushdie for allegedly blaspheming Islam in his book "The Satanic Verses."
Insisting "We are law-abiding citizens," he said British Moslems would like to pursue criminal proceedings against Rushdie and his publisher through the courts.

Proposing a 10-point Bill of Rights, he said Moslems should enjoy the same protection afforded Christians. "The current surge in Islamophobia seeks to divide society, portraying an incorrect image of a barbaric and backward Islam," he said.
He complained that Britain's 1967 race relations act only protected ethnic minorities. None was offered to religious minorities and the law should be changed, he said.
Pasha also called on the government to fund Moslem schools, allow Moslems to perform their prayers at work and let them have two national statutory holidays a year.
He preached integration, not assimilation. "We are now part and parcel of British society," he said.

Warning of the dangers of drugs, alcoholism and teenage pregnancies in British schools, the union said in a statement of its policies: "The danger that assimilation poses is far more serious than the authorities visualise.

"A young generation which is uprooted from its cultural roots will easily succumb to the temptations of a secular and promiscuous society and cause sociological problems whose containment might prove costly and divisive."
